IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
The $2.8 billion package is real and is funded entirely by the Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program, which uses American taxpayer funds to allow Israel to purchase US-made weapons. Biden's pause covered a single shipment of 2,000-pound bombs in May 2024, motivated by concerns about their use in Rafah. Trump lifted that pause a few weeks after taking office in January 2025.

The Contents of the Package

The $2.8 billion covers 40,000 2,000-pound bombs: 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s, plus 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator armor-piercing warheads designed to strike underground structures. An MK-84 can kill at over 300 meters from the detonation point and create a crater 15 meters wide and 11 meters deep. A Harvard FXB Center study found that between October and November 2023, Israel dropped nearly 600 2,000-pound bombs, a third of which were within lethal range of Gaza hospitals.

The "Gift" Mechanism

The FMF program provides Israel with subsidies to purchase American weapons. The practical result is that the cost of the bombs is covered by the US federal budget, while the bombs are produced by American defense companies and delivered to Israel. Tucker Carlson called the package "the largest transfer of conventional explosive devices in modern history" and a "taxpayer-funded gift." Marjorie Taylor Greene wrote in X: "We didn't vote for this. America doesn't support this. Our tax dollars and our weapons have been used to kill tens of thousands of innocent people."

The Political and Legal Context

The sale has been informally notified to the relevant congressional committees, but has not yet completed the formal process. Congress can attempt to block it, but an opposing resolution would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto. The Secretary of State has circumvented congressional review in the past by using emergency powers to approve similar packages.

The timing is significant: the package comes as the United States has consumed a record amount of munitions in the war with Iran, with $22.3 billion spent on munitions between February and June 2026, depleting the Pentagon's strategic stockpile.

quotedTweet.text:
Outraged about the US sending Israel more bombs? Wait till you find out who's paying for them.

The $2.8 billion isn't Israel buying weapons from us with their own money. It's American taxpayer dollars, funneled through a program called Foreign Military Financing, so Israel can receive 40,000 more 2,000-pound bombs. We are paying for our own bombs to be handed to them, for free, on our dime.

Biden paused this exact shipment back in 2024 because of what these bombs do — MK-84s and BLU-117s have a blast radius wide enough to level a city block, and Israel had already been using them in Gaza's most crowded neighborhoods, sometimes killing dozens of civilians to hit one target. Trump reversed that pause days after taking office.

Now his administration wants to send 40,000 more, plus bunker-busting penetrator warheads, and American taxpayers are covering the entire tab, in dollars and reputation.

The damage from these bombs isn't hypothetical. It's already documented, condemned by human rights groups and foreign governments alike. And the response to that damage is to buy 40,000 more and give them away, funded entirely by us.

Even Tucker Carlson is calling this a "gift" at Americans' expense. Marjorie Taylor Greene says flatly: "we did not vote for this."

text:
In 2021 I got tired of rebuilding login, tenants and caching on every new .NET project. So I built it once, in the open.

That became FullStackHero: a free, MIT-licensed .NET 10 starter kit for multi-tenant SaaS apps and APIs.

Five years later it has 6,700+ stars on GitHub, almost 2,000 forks and 2,500+ commits.

The problem it solves is boring on purpose. Every serious app needs the same unglamorous 80% before it does anything interesting: auth, tenants, audit logs, jobs, file storage, API docs.

That plumbing usually eats the first month. With the kit, day one is feature work.

v10 is a ground-up rebuild. The old version was two repos, a .NET 6 Clean Architecture API and a Blazor client. Redoing it properly took months.

Now it's one modular monolith. That means ten modules in one codebase, deployed as one app, but each module owns its own database context and folders.

The ten: Identity, Multitenancy, Auditing, Webhooks, Files, Notifications, Billing, Catalog, Chat and Tickets.

Inside a module, every feature is a vertical slice. Registering a user is one folder, with the endpoint sitting right next to its handler and validator. No jumping across layers to add one endpoint.

The rule I care about most: modules never reference each other. They only talk through a thin Contracts project that holds commands, queries, events and DTOs.

Architecture tests enforce that. Break a boundary and the build goes red, so the design can't quietly rot.

When one module needs to tell another something, it writes an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as its own save. If you ever split a module into its own service, those boundaries are exactly where you cut.

Running it is one command. Aspire starts Postgres, Valkey, MinIO, the API and both React 19 apps, seeded with two demo tenants. 1,600+ backend tests and 200+ end-to-end tests sit behind it.

It's also built for AI agents. Claude can generate a backend from one prompt, but it won't reliably decide where boundaries sit or how tenancy flows into caching and jobs. The kit ships an AGENTS file with rules and skills, so the agent follows the architecture instead of guessing.

Honest caveat: it's opinionated and ships a lot. For a small internal tool or a single microservice, it's over-engineered.

Pick it when those ten modules are roughly the ten you were about to build anyway.

Save this for the next project where you're about to spend a sprint wiring login and tenants from scratch.

Happy Coding :)

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

text:
Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

Until then, PROGA’s criminal prohibitions remain fully operative.
Law changed — but risk calculus didn’t.

#PROGA2025 #OnlineGamingLaw #RMG #ITRules2026 #LegalAnalysis #GamingRegulationIndia

An Early DIC Initiative from the Media Lab Asia Era That Helped Shape India’s Digital Journey.

Building a digital knowledge ecosystem for agriculture and rural livelihoods.

Developed with IIT Kanpur, Krishi Vigyan Kendras and rural institutions, DEAL enabled farmers, experts and communities to create, organise, share and reuse agricultural knowledge across networks.

Through multimedia repositories, Hindi & English content, an agricultural ontology, Voice/Kisan Blog, and expert knowledge sharing, the initiative strengthened community-driven access to knowledge.

Knowledge Created. Knowledge Shared. Communities Empowered.

PM Modi Celebrates 76th Birthday

Here are the key moments that defined India’s digital revolution under Modi’s leadership:

🔸2014: Jan Dhan brings millions into formal banking, backed by Aadhaar and mobile connectivity

🔸2015: Digital India expands digital infrastructure and online public services

🔸2016: UPI enables instant, interoperable digital payments

🔸2020–21: Electronics manufacturing gets a major boost through PLI, while the National Single Window System streamlines business approvals

🔸2021: The $7.92B Semicon India Programme lays the foundation for domestic chip manufacturing and design

🔸2024: The $1.08B IndiaAI Mission targets AI compute, datasets, innovation and applications

From bank accounts and digital identity to UPI, smartphones, AI and semiconductors, India’s digital journey has moved from expanding access to building strategic technology capabilities.

The next phase: AI, chips and deeper digital sovereignty.

From early innovation to digital transformation at scale, Digital India Corporation’s mission continues to evolve with India.

Today, DIC’s work spans five interconnected areas:

Women, Children & Social Empowerment
Agriculture & Livelihoods
Education
Youth Empowerment, Nationhood & Culture
Digital Governance & Infrastructure

Together, these areas reflect technology's expanding role in empowering people, strengthening systems and creating public impact.

Five Areas. One Continuing Mission.

14th September 2026 shall be remembered as a day of “Digital Somersault” and also 
as a day of “Betrayal & Surrender” by the Union BJP Govt, as it opened the door for 
imposing a “UPI Transaction Tax” on UPI transactions above Rs. 2000, with effect 
from 15th October 2026. The Govt and the National Payments Corporation of India 
(NPCI) are presently putting the charge at 0.4% for P2M (Person-to-Merchant) 
transactions.

IMPOSITION OF UPI TRANSACTION TAX IS BETRAYAL-BACKSTABBING-
DOUBLE CROSSING OF PEOPLE OF INDIA 

In two separate PIB Press releases dated 30th April 2026 & 24th August 2026,the Modi Govt has admitted that in the year 2025-26, there were 24,162 Crore

🔰UPI Payments to Remain Free for Person to Person transactions; MDR Applicable Only on Large-Value Merchant Transactions

▪️The Government has amended the Payment and Settlement Systems (PSS) Act, 2007 empowering the government to notify specific electronic payment modes where no charges shall apply. 

▪️This amendment provides the legal foundation to ensure affordability and transparency in digital transactions 

▪️On 14 September 2026, the Central Government issued a notification under this framework, specifying that Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions up to ₹2,000 will attract zero Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) 

▪️Further, detailed circular has also been issued by NPCI on 15th September, 2026, after deliberation of UPI steering committee on operational parameters, fee distribution models, and category caps 

🔰The key highlights of the circular are as follows:

▪️For person-to-person (P2P) transactions, there will be no charges at all, irrespective of transaction value. P2P transactions constitute 37% of the total UPI transactions in volume terms and 70% in value terms

▪️Charges will apply only to person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions exceeding ₹2,000 

🔰Technical Framework

▪️A nominal MDR of 0.4% will be levied on P2M transactions above ₹2,000. This commission will be shared amongst the payment ecosystem partners, including banks and app providers

▪️For high-value transactions of ₹75,000 and above, MDR will be capped at ₹300 per transaction

शब्द जो नीति बने: बीते बारह वर्षों की शासन-शब्दावली
शासन की भाषा प्रायः फ़ाइलों, विभागों और योजनाओं के नामों तक सीमित रहती है। 2014 के बाद भारत की राजनीतिक भाषा में एक असामान्य बदलाव आया - ऐसे शब्द जो पहले केवल विशेषज्ञों की गोष्ठियों, तकनीकी पत्रिकाओं या विदेशी सम्मेलनों में सुनाई देते थे, अचानक लाल किले के भाषणों, बजट की मदों और गाँव-कस्बों के होर्डिंग तक पहुँच गए। और उससे भी अहम - वे शब्द केवल नारे नहीं रहे; उनके पीछे मिशन, बजट, समय-सीमा और ज़मीन पर दिखने वाली परियोजनाएँ खड़ी हुईं। समर्थकों का दावा यही है कि इस शब्दावली और उसके क्रियान्वयन में ही इस नेतृत्व की अभूतपूर्वता छिपी है।

1. डिजिटल और प्रौद्योगिकी की शब्दावली
Digital India (2015) से शुरू हुई यात्रा ने JAM त्रिमूर्ति (जन धन-आधार-मोबाइल) और DBT (प्रत्यक्ष लाभ अंतरण) को आम आदमी की भाषा बनाया। UPI ने "स्कैन करो" को देश का क्रिया-शब्द बना दिया। India Stack और Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) - यह शब्द 2023 की G20 अध्यक्षता में भारत ने दुनिया की नीति-शब्दावली में दर्ज कराया। ONDC, Account Aggregator, CoWIN, Aarogya Setu, e-Sanjeevani, Digital Rupee (CBDC) - हर शब्द के पीछे एक चालू प्लेटफ़ॉर्म है।
5G (2022 में लॉन्च) के साथ Bharat 6G Vision (2023), इस दशक को "Techade" कहना, National Quantum Mission (2023), IndiaAI Mission (2024) और फरवरी 2026 में दिल्ली में AI Impact Summit की मेज़बानी - ये सब उस नेतृत्व की भाषा है जिसने "AI" को चुनावी भाषण में लाने का जोखिम उठाया। Semiconductor - India Semiconductor Mission (2021), Semicon India, धोलेरा और साणंद की इकाइयाँ, 2025 में पहली मेड-इन-इंडिया चिपों का प्रस्तुत होना - चार दशक पुराना सपना पहली बार बजट की मद बना। Drone Rules, Namo Drone Didi, Agri Stack, Data Centre नीति और Deep Tech Fund इसी सूची के विस्तार हैं।

2. उद्योग, अवसंरचना और लॉजिस्टिक्स
Make in India (2014), Zero Defect Zero Effect, PLI (उत्पादन-आधारित प्रोत्साहन), Startup India और Unicorn - "स्टार्टअप" शब्द को शहरों से निकालकर टियर-2 और टियर-3 तक पहुँचाना इसी दौर की देन है। Defence Corridor (2018, उत्तर प्रदेश और तमिलनाडु) और Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) ने रक्षा-निर्यात को राजनीतिक विमर्श का विषय बनाया। Vocal for Local, Ease of Doing Business और Ease of Living - दोनों को जोड़कर देखना नई बात थी।
PM Gati Shakti (2021) ने Multi-Modal Connectivity को - सड़क, रेल, बंदरगाह, हवाई अड्डा और डेटा एक ही नक़्शे पर - नीति का केंद्र बनाया; National Logistics Policy (2022) उसी की पूरक है। Bharatmala, Sagarmala, UDAN, Vande Bharat, Dedicated Freight Corridor, Bullet Train, Smart Cities, Amrit Bharat Station, Blue Economy, Maritime Development Fund, GIFT City, IMEC (भारत–मध्य-पूर्व–यूरोप कॉरिडोर, 2023), Purvodaya, National Manufacturing Mission (2025), Critical Minerals Mission (2025) और Nuclear Energy Mission / SMR (छोटे मॉड्यूलर रिएक्टर) - यह सूची एक ऐसे राजनेता की है जो इंजीनियरिंग के शब्दों में राजनीति करता है।

3. ऊर्जा और पर्यावरण
International Solar Alliance (2015, पेरिस), Panchamrit और Net Zero 2070 (ग्लासगो, 2021), Mission LiFE (पर्यावरण-अनुकूल जीवनशैली), Green Hydrogen Mission (2023), Green Growth, Circular Economy, Waste to Wealth, Ethanol Blending, PM Surya Ghar (छत पर सौर, 2024), Deep Ocean Mission / Samudrayaan, Mission Mausam और Global Biofuel Alliance (2023)। "हाइड्रोजन" और "सर्कुलर इकॉनमी" जैसे शब्दों को प्रधानमंत्री के मुँह से सुनना पहले कल्पना से बाहर था।

4. समाज और कल्याण की नई भाषा
Swachh Bharat, Ujjwala, Jan Dhan, Ayushman Bharat, Har Ghar Jal, Aspirational Districts (डेटा-आधारित प्रतिस्पर्धी शासन), Saturation (हर पात्र तक पहुँच), Lakhpati Didi, Nari Shakti (महिला आरक्षण अधिनियम, 2023), PM Vishwakarma, SVAMITVA (ड्रोन से गाँव की ज़मीन का नक़्शा), Shree Anna (मिलेट्स को वैश्विक मंच), Mission Karmayogi, Skill India, Khelo India, Fit India, Yoga Day, Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat, Har Ghar Tiranga।

5. शासन-दर्शन के शब्द
Minimum Government, Maximum Governance; Reform, Perform, Transform; Cooperative और Competitive Federalism (NITI Aayog, 2015); Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas; Jan Bhagidari; One Nation One Tax (GST), One Nation One Ration Card, One Nation One Election; Amrit Kaal, Panch Pran, Viksit Bharat 2047, Vikas bhi, Virasat bhi।

6. वैश्विक मंच पर
Neighbourhood First, Act East, Vaccine Maitri, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (G20 की थीम), Voice of Global South, अफ्रीकी संघ को G20 में स्थायी सदस्यता, CDRI (आपदा-सह अवसंरचना गठबंधन)। "ग्लोबल साउथ" शब्द को भारत ने अपनी कूटनीति का ब्रांड बनाया।

क्यों "अभूतपूर्व"?
पहला - शब्द नीति से पहले आया और नीति को दिशा दी। पहले योजनाएँ बनती थीं और नाम बाद में; यहाँ पहले एक भविष्य-दृष्टि का शब्द आया (सेमीकंडक्टर, हाइड्रोजन, क्वांटम, गति शक्ति) और फिर उसके पीछे मिशन, धन और समय-सीमा खड़ी की गई।

दूसरा - पैमाना और गति। UPI का लेनदेन, जन धन खाते, DBT से बचत, वंदे भारत की संख्या, सौर क्षमता - ये आँकड़े शब्दों को खोखला नारा नहीं रहने देते।

तीसरा - विपरीत पक्ष की भाषा का ठहराव।जब सत्ता की शब्दावली "क्वांटम", "ग्रीन हाइड्रोजन" और "डिफेंस कॉरिडोर" की है, तब विपक्ष की राजनीतिक व्याकरण अब भी परिवार, विरासत, उपनाम और "हमारे समय में" पर टिकी है। भविष्य की भाषा और अतीत की भाषा के बीच यही अंतर, इस नेतृत्व को अभूतपूर्व बनाता है।

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Statement on Automated Takedown of Its Instagram Posts by Meta

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

California is asking experts how the most powerful AI models could be shut off in an emergency. Governor Newsom's September eighteen executive order accelerates independent verification and auditor laws, while requesting safety recommendations within two months. An emergency shutoff is among the proposals being considered, so this is a push to develop safeguards rather than a blanket shutdown requirement already imposed.

Businesses speaking to the Richmond Fed say AI is continuing to slow hiring, especially for white-collar jobs. Its September eighteen outreach report also says several firms are hiring people with AI-specific skills, while most expect flat or growing headcounts by year-end. Some firms say AI could help cut staffing if demand contracts, but these regional contacts are not a national estimate of job losses.

An AI-assisted intelligence report nearly led the American military to intercept a Chinese vessel, according to CNN's sources. CNN's September eighteen disclosure describes an incident in spring when military planes were already airborne before officials discovered that a chatbot had misidentified the cargo. The error was caught before the operation, while the model and the actual cargo remain unidentified in the report.

California's new advertising law requires viewers and listeners to be told when a selling performance is AI-generated. Newsom signed the measure on September sixteen, covering video and audio advertisements that use AI-generated performers to sell products or services. The governor's release says advertisements violating the law cannot continue running, although it does not establish an effective date for this report.

A lawsuit claims that a coordinated AI slowdown has reduced what subscribers receive for their money. According to the Associated Press, the September eighteen filing accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google of an unlawful coordinated slowdown. The claimed loss of subscription value is the plaintiffs' allegation, and the filing does not establish that the companies broke the law.

Egypt and Intel plan to bring AI education to one million citizens a year. The partnership reported on September sixteen sets that annual target for three years, following an agreement with Egypt's communications ministry. Its planned lessons cover basic AI concepts and safe, responsible technology use, with those participation numbers representing goals rather than completed training.

Nineteen European Union countries have designed a joint project intended to make AI technologies and services more widely accessible. The European Commission's September sixteen announcement describes the German-coordinated design and says eleven states plan to begin submitting state-aid projects for preliminary review in September. The ambition is shared, decentralised AI services, but funding still requires assessment and this announcement does not mean those services are already deployed.

Tether says its translation models for nineteen African languages can work offline on ordinary phones. The September two announcement introduced TranslatePsy-AfriSLM resources, with model weights and inference code available and a separately licensed synthetic dataset for non-commercial research and education. Offline operation could remove the need for an internet connection during translation, although that capability is the company's claim rather than an independently verified result here.

Craif says it has completed enrollment and sample collection for a pivotal trial of AI software that uses urine biomarkers to support pancreatic-cancer diagnosis. The September seventeen announcement concerns a study begun in April twenty twenty-four across twelve Japanese facilities, with analysis and an application planned this year and approval targeted for twenty twenty-seven. The proposed device would help clinicians decide which patients with suspected pancreatic cancer and risk factors need detailed tests, but the milestone is neither an efficacy result nor an approval.

Qure says its Aira clinical assistant has received European Class Two B medical-device certification for clinical decision support. The September eighteen announcement describes a system combining documentation, workflow automation and patient-record analysis with clinical recommendations based on guidelines. The company reports ten live pilot sites across five countries, bringing the system into clinical workflows while the certification and pilot outcomes remain company-reported in the evidence reviewed.

Retail robots in a Japanese demonstration are testing AI computing roughly five hundred kilometres away. KDDI, Morgenrot and Tohknet announced the distributed-data-centre demonstration on September eighteen, connecting geographically separated resources over high-speed networks. The project aims to ease electricity and computing-chip shortages by sharing distant capacity, although a demonstration does not establish commercial savings or deployment.

KDDI is offering businesses help building tailored AI agents with Gemini Enterprise. The service launched September eighteen combines licenses, development by KDDI iret and private-network connectivity, with proposed tasks ranging from information gathering to reports and approval workflows. Customers need a cloudpack with KDDI contract, and the proposed automation should not be mistaken for independently demonstrated productivity gains.

Huawei has announced its latest AI Cluster Service alongside new government and AI hardware partnership zones. Its September eighteen announcement schedules commercial availability of the cluster service for September thirty in China and November thirty outside China. Huawei says twenty-four founding partners in the government zone cover public services, office operations and urban governance, making those areas a focus of its planned expansion.

Convano's AXON concept proposes using AI and speech recognition to handle medical administration. The company says it first outlined the concept on September ten, followed by a September eighteen announcement of a detailed online briefing. The planned system would assist appointment booking, record preparation and other non-clinical work, but these remain proposed tasks without implementation results.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

They’re from the $250M DFW gold scam case. Reading court filings in the case proves the immigration angle is almost as wild as the scam itself.

Start with the people around the jewelry operation:

Rafiq Sajwani: came from Pakistan in 2018 on an EB-5 investor visa, later became a permanent resident, and was recruited to work at Malani Jewelers.

Sunil Keshavan Nair: came from India in 2012 and became a U.S. citizen in 2021. Investigators allege he participated in undocumented gold purchases and used $1 bills as “tokens” in what they described as a hawala network.

Tithi Patel: Gujarati reporting says she entered on a student visa and overstayed before working around Tilak Jewelers. 

Multiple other defendants: booking records show immigration detainers or other foreign-national indicators.

Then there’s the IT-company angle. (shocker, I know)

The State alleges Shermyn Malani owned an IT company associated with the Georgia jewelry operation. Investigators also described IT companies in the broader case as being used for “visa fraud and money laundering.”

But wait, there’s more - a confidential source separately accused the Malanis of hiring illegal immigrants.

Now zoom out.

Authorities allege elderly Americans were frightened into converting their savings into gold and cash.

Couriers then collected it.  

Jewelry stores allegedly bought the gold below market and melted it, making the victim trail harder to follow.

Investigators describe shell companies, crypto, informal money-transfer mechanisms and overseas connections.

Then you get to the people running the jewelry businesses.

Iqbal and Shermyn Malani happen to be American-Canadian dual citizens, but unlike what you and I think of when we think Canadian, their overseas connection aren’t merely ancestral.

Iqbal, Shermyn and other Malani family members have served as directors of an Indian company in Hyderabad.

Now - here’s the part I didn’t expect.

In court, the Malanis’ family testified that Iqbal held a prestigious spiritual-leadership position in their religious community, Shermyn taught children there and the couple had donated more than $10 million to charity.

Malani Jewelers’ own website identifies the Aga Khan Foundation / Aga Khan Development Network as its primary international charitable relationship and says purchases at Malani Jewelers contribute to its charitable giving programs.

Tl/dr.

We have an alleged fraud in which American seniors’ wealth was converted into gold.

Investigators allege that gold entered jewelry businesses.

Those businesses sit inside a family network with direct overseas corporate ties.

The investigation itself contains allegations involving visa fraud, immigration violations, IT companies and difficult-to-trace international money movement.

And the jewelry company publicly says its business supports a transnational religious/philanthropic network.

The biggest question I’m left with, among many others is: 

How many people entered or remained in the U.S. through visa programs, got plugged into this business network and then ended up inside an alleged fraud that moved American seniors’ wealth overseas?
