text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text: @SachdevaAmita @nealmohan Why are @YouTube @nealmohan not complying with the Order of the Grievance Appellate Committee?

“Maybe Maa Sita Blessed Her To Take This Action”
Kudos And Congratulations Amita Ji

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. The dispute centers around a video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED”, which Rathee uploaded in March.

Advocate @SachdevaAmita (Amita Sachdeva) filed a petition alleging that the video contained “false, misleading, and provocative statements” claiming that Hindu deities Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol. She argued this severely hurt the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus.

Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

#HearingUpdate Shaban Alam v. UOI & Ors. W.P.(C) No. 13044/2026, is listed tomorrow before HMJ Dr. Swarana Kanta Sharma of the Hon'ble DHC. The petition challenges the order of the Grievance Appellate Committee estd. u/R 3A of the IT Rules 2021. https://t.co/XzbMJ8iVNx

text:
🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.
Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

THE COPYRIGHT STAKES IN THE EU–INDIA FTA

Introduction

The article by Zakir Thomas and Biswajit Dhar examines how the proposed India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) could affect India’s copyright regime, particularly the balance between IP protection and public-interest exceptions.

Main Facts

The draft IP chapter reportedly contains copyright provisions that may require changes to India’s Copyright Act, 1957.

India’s existing framework provides important exceptions for education, research, libraries, archives and digital intermediaries.

The article argues that the draft may weaken these flexibilities by incorporating stronger enforcement obligations.

The WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT) is important because it balances authors’ rights with legitimate public-interest uses in the digital environment.

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) currently receive statutory safe-harbour protection for certain transient/technical copies.

Challenges

Digital rights management (DRM) and strict anti-circumvention rules could restrict legitimate educational and research activities.

Students and cybersecurity researchers may face difficulties in reverse-engineering software for lawful purposes.

Libraries and archives could face obstacles in format-shifting and digital preservation.

Reduced intermediary safe harbours could increase legal uncertainty for digital platforms.

Constructive Criticism

The article highlights a fundamental policy dilemma: excessive copyright enforcement can protect private IP rights while simultaneously constraining access to knowledge, education, research and innovation.

Way Forward

Preserve India’s copyright exceptions and limitations.

Ensure any FTA commitments remain consistent with India’s domestic legislative mandate.

Retain appropriate WCT flexibility, including public-interest safeguards.

Protect legitimate educational, archival and cybersecurity activities.

Maintain proportionate intermediary safe harbours.

Highlighted Keywords

Copyright | Intellectual Property | WCT | FTA | Fair Dealing | DRM | Anti-Circumvention | Safe Harbour | Digital Sovereignty | Access to Knowledge

Conclusion

The core issue is not IP protection versus free trade, but achieving an equilibrium between innovation incentives and public access to knowledge. India’s digital economy requires copyright rules that protect creators without suffocating education, research and technological innovation.

Had a very insightful call yesterday with APR Technologies CEO Lars Almhem, founder and former CEO Peter Nilsson, and AAIG with @Mark_AAIG  and @MarkosAAIG .

Here is roughly where the $APRTEC thesis stands today.

APRTEC is a small Swedish team tackling liquid cooling problems with its EHD technology.

The main focus increasingly appears to be data center cooling, putting them in roughly the same arena as Accelsius, $INV and ZutaCore.

But the technology reaches much further.

They already sell space cooling applications and appear close to signing a commercial agreement with Zoppas.

They also have battery cooling solutions using immersion cooling, for applications such as drone batteries.

Beyond that, they clearly have their eyes on areas such as HBM, photonics and lasers, although the limiting factor today seems to be resources rather than opportunity.

The company has a very promising technical team and R&D background.

The main question is now simple:

Can they scale manufacturing and actually sell the technology?

If they can, I think the story has genuine 20x+ potential.

And some of the newest datapoints are starting to make that scenario more tangible.

When asked about factory expansion, management said they already have preliminary plans for a second and third factory, likely outside Sweden.

One factory represents roughly 500k units of annual capacity.

Blended unit pricing is now expected to be around $75 to $100.

That means the manufacturing footprint they are already thinking about could eventually support a very substantial revenue base.

Peter also said that the volume ramp is going very well so far.

We also know APR is in discussions with several large technology customers and hyperscalers.

One customer has already placed a pre production order, which has been delivered, and the product is now in field testing.

It is still difficult to know the exact timeline or whether this turns into a large volume order.

But what we do know is that a very large customer has already spent meaningful time and resources evaluating the technology.

Given that volume production is expected to begin in 2027, I would not be surprised if we get much more clarity over the next quarter or two.

Another interesting development is retrofit.

Historically APR has focused much more heavily on getting designed into new systems early in the development process.

They are now actively looking at retrofit opportunities as well.

Definitely something to watch.

The team is also expanding across operations, quality and sales, exactly the functions you would expect them to strengthen ahead of a manufacturing ramp.

And importantly, management has now confirmed gross margins above 50%.

That matters enormously for the long term valuation framework.

So the thesis remains very asymmetric.

The technology looks increasingly credible.

The commercial pipeline appears real.

Manufacturing capacity is being planned beyond the first factory.

Margins look excellent.

Now they need to prove that qualification turns into real volume.

I’ll publish more of the research later on my Substack, and we will likely also see deeper work from AAIG on their platform.

I’ll also update my original deep dive with the newest information.

For now I’ll link the older piece below.

And if you are interested in liquid cooling more broadly, definitely check out AAIG’s work on the other names in the space. $INV $APRTEC.ST $APRTEC $NBIS $VRT $DELL

A guy who sold $1.2 million on Amazon last year told me his biggest secret.

Nothing he sells is his.

Not one product. Not one design. Not one idea.

The $35 earbuds? $3.80 from a factory.

The $28 phone case? $1.40.
The $45 desk lamp? $6.20.
The $22 resistance bands? $0.90.
440% markup. On every product. Every day. For 4 years.

His entire business is a logo and a listing.

"I open Alibaba. I find what already sells on Amazon. I order 500 units with my logo. The factory ships them to Amazon. Amazon sells them. I never touch the product. Never see it. Never store it. I just keep the margin."

That's it. That's a $1.2 million business.

"And the factory that makes my earbuds? They make 14 other 'brands' of the same earbud. Same line. Same mold. Same box. 14 logos. 14 prices. $19 to $59. Identical product."

"But here's what should change how you shop forever that factory will sell to you. Right now. For $3.80. No license. No registration. No minimum order. You message them. They reply in minutes. You pay. They ship."

"The only thing separating you from factory prices is that you never opened Alibaba. That's it. That's the entire wall."

Here are 10 things most people get wrong about buying from Alibaba and the exact playbook for buying factory-direct:

🧵

HE ADMITTED THE QUALITY IS IDENTICAL — Because he can't change the quality. The factory controls the mold, the materials, and the production line. He just controls the logo.

He said this is the part most Amazon sellers won't say out loud.

"I don't control the quality. The factory does. I chose a factory with a quality level I was satisfied with. I approved the sample. I approved the production run. But the product itself — the engineering, the materials, the tolerances, the components — is entirely the factory's work. I added a logo. That's my contribution."

He said the factory sells the identical product — same quality — to any buyer who messages them.

"The factory doesn't make a 'premium version' for me and a 'budget version' for random buyers. They make one product. On one production line. With one set of materials. My logo goes on 500 units. Another seller's logo goes on 500 units. A consumer who orders 50 units with no logo gets the same product from the same batch. The quality is identical because the factory is identical."

He said he's compared his own Amazon product against the same product bought directly from the factory — side by side.

"Same weight on a kitchen scale. Same driver response on a frequency analyzer. Same Bluetooth connection speed. Same battery life. Same charging time. Same fit. Same sound. The logo was the only difference. On one pair, it said his brand name. On the other, it said nothing. $34.99 versus $3.80. For a logo printed in a font he chose on Canva."

THE FACTORY WILL SELL TO ANYONE — No license. No business registration. No minimum in many cases. You message them. They reply. That's the entire process.

He said this is the fact that breaks people's understanding of how commerce works.

"Alibaba is not a wholesale-only platform. It's a directory of factories with a search bar and a 'Contact Supplier' button. The factories list their products, their prices, their capabilities, and their minimum orders. Anyone on Earth can message them. The factory doesn't ask if you're a business. They don't ask for a resale license. They ask: 'How many do you want? Where should we ship?'"

He said 70% of factories accept trial orders well below their listed minimum.

"The listing says MOQ: 500. You message and say: 'I'd like to start with 50 units as a trial order. Is that possible?' Seven out of ten factories say yes. The per-unit price is 10–30% higher at 50 units than at 500 — but even at the premium price, you're paying 80–90% less than Amazon retail."

He said Ready to Ship products eliminate the MOQ entirely.

"On Alibaba, filter by 'Ready to Ship.' These are pre-made products in stock at the factory — ready to ship immediately, often with no minimum order. Some are available in quantities of 1–10. The prices are slightly higher than custom bulk orders — but there's no production wait, no MOQ negotiation, and no factory relationship to build. You buy it like Amazon. It arrives in 7–15 days. Except the price is 85% lower."

This video presents a strongly critical argument about India’s electoral-roll revisions, alleging that the BJP government is using laws and institutions to reshape the electorate. It cites The Japan Times, political analyst Yogendra Yadav and French political scientist Gilles Vernier, among others. 

It further claims that 65 million voters have been removed across nine states, with the number potentially reaching 100 million. Those figures and the political interpretation should be understood as claims reported in the video, rather than presented as independently established facts. 

THE BIGGER ISSUE: WHO GETS TO REMAIN ON THE ELECTORAL ROLL?

The Election Commission says the purpose of SIR is to ensure that no eligible citizen is excluded and no ineligible person is included. It says deletions are based on categories including death, permanent shifting, duplicate entries and voters who remain untraceable after repeated verification. 

At the same time, the scale of the exercise makes independent scrutiny and transparent verification essential.

The ECI's own stated constitutional responsibility is to maintain the integrity of electoral rolls and conduct elections in accordance with the constitutional and statutory framework. 

That creates a fundamental democratic test:

Can the system remove ineligible entries without disenfranchising eligible citizens—and can every disputed deletion be effectively challenged?

THIS IS BIGGER THAN ONE PARTY

Whether one agrees with the video's political interpretation or not, electoral-roll revision affects something more fundamental than party politics:

the citizen's right to participate in choosing government.

That is why every deletion should be:

VERIFIABLE.
EXPLAINABLE.
APPEALABLE.
TRANSPARENT.

And criticism of the process should be answered with data, documentation and due process—not dismissal of the question itself.

The Supreme Court has also examined the legal framework surrounding SIR; reporting on its May 2026 judgment says the Court upheld the ECI's authority to conduct the exercise while the broader implementation questions remain matters of public scrutiny. 

UNITED RESISTANCE — FOR THE RIGHT TO VOTE

United resistance need not mean unquestioning agreement on every political claim.

It can mean something simpler:

Different parties. Different ideologies. One common democratic demand—no eligible citizen should lose the right to vote through an opaque or uncorrectable process.

Protect the voter. Protect the electoral roll. Protect the constitutional process.

The video by Abhijeet Dipke uses sharp political satire to imagine an extreme scenario: the Election Commission openly joining the ruling party, opposition parties being dissolved, their election symbols being frozen, and only one party being permitted to contest elections. 

The exaggeration is deliberate—but the underlying question is serious:

What happens to democracy when citizens stop believing that the institution conducting elections is politically impartial?

THE INSTITUTION MATTERS

The Election Commission of India is a constitutional authority responsible for administering elections to Parliament and State Legislatures. Article 324 gives it superintendence, direction and control over elections. The ECI also regulates recognition of political parties and allotment of election symbols under the Election Symbols Order, 1968. 

That institutional role makes perceived neutrality as important as formal constitutional powers.

A democracy does not depend merely on the existence of polling booths, EVMs or election dates. It also depends upon public confidence that competing political parties are operating under rules that are applied fairly.

THE SATIRE'S WARNING

The video's imagined solution—dissolve the opposition, freeze their symbols and allow only one party to contest—is obviously presented as an extreme proposition. 

But that is precisely why the satire lands:

If an election institution is perceived as favouring one political side, the problem is bigger than one election. It becomes a question about institutional legitimacy itself.

The ECI officially describes India's system as a constitutional democracy committed to regular, free and fair elections. 

The democratic standard, therefore, should be simple:

The referee must be trusted by the players—and, above all, by the public.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

Timsy Jaipuria, a former CNBC-TV18 economic policy journalist, recounts what happened after the Prime Minister publicly rejected one of her reports in May 2026.

Her account raises a fundamental question about journalism: Is reporting government discussions itself a mistake simply because a government may later deny them?

Jaipuria says the report was based on multiple-source verification and that she had emailed the Finance Ministry, PIB and Revenue Secretary hours before the story went on air, seeking their version.

She also makes an important distinction: she describes the Prime Minister's post as a denial, not a fact-check, because no contrary evidence was presented to establish that the reported discussion had not taken place.

Most revealing is what followed. The story was pulled down, she faced intense personal trolling, gradually stopped appearing on air, and eventually resigned after completing her notice period.

Yet she says she would still stand by the journalism behind the report.

That is the larger issue.

A healthy democracy needs journalists who can report what governments are considering—not merely repeat what governments have already decided.

When power publicly challenges a journalist, the real test is not whether the journalist is powerful enough to fight back.

It is whether journalism remains free enough to ask the next question.

Who watches power when journalists are made afraid to report what power is thinking?

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
Jagtar Singh Johal and Mazi Nnamdi Kanu: Why Their Legal Positions Differ.

Both are British citizens, but extraordinary rendition, conviction and their current procedural positions make these two cases legally distinct.

21 September 2026

The most important difference between the cases of Jagtar Singh Johal and my husband, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, is not British citizenship.

Both men are British citizens.

The more important distinction, as of 21 September 2026, is where each man now stands in the criminal process, and, critically, how each came into custody.

Johal has now been granted bail after spending more than eight years largely in pre-trial detention in India. In its judgment of 18 September 2026, the Delhi High Court recorded that only 40 prosecution witnesses had been examined and that another 123 witnesses remained. The court concluded that the trials were unlikely to finish soon and ordered his release on bail subject to substantial conditions, including surrender of his passport.

Mazi Nnamdi Kanu is in a different procedural position. On 20 November 2025, Nigeria's Federal High Court convicted him on all seven counts before it and imposed life imprisonment on multiple counts, together with additional prison terms. He is appealing those convictions and sentences.

His application for bail pending appeal, filed on 5 June 2026, was still being publicly described as pending in late August, and reporting in September continued to describe the substantive appeal as awaiting determination.

That makes the present bail questions legally different.

But there is another difference, one that deserves particular attention.

Kanu's Case Has an Additional Issue: Extraordinary Rendition Across an International Border

There is one particularly important feature of Mazi Nnamdi Kanu's case that does not arise in Johal's case in the same form:

extraordinary rendition across an international border.

Kanu was taken in Kenya in June 2021 and brought to Nigeria outside the ordinary extradition process.

The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention subsequently found that he had been subjected to extraordinary rendition and concluded that his detention was arbitrary.

This is not simply an allegation made by his family or lawyers. The circumstances of his removal have subsequently been addressed by courts in both Nigeria and Kenya.

What Nigeria's Court of Appeal Decided in 2022

In October 2022, Nigeria's Court of Appeal held that the manner in which Kanu had been brought back from Kenya was unlawful.

The court concluded that the Federal Government had violated the law in forcibly returning him to Nigeria and held that the trial could not proceed on the basis then before it. It discharged him.

At that point, the legal consequence attached to the unlawful rendition was extremely significant.

But that was not the end of the story.

What Nigeria's Supreme Court Decided in December 2023

On 15 December 2023, Nigeria's Supreme Court reversed the consequence reached by the Court of Appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court did not simply declare that everything surrounding Kanu's return from Kenya had been lawful.

Reporting on the judgment records that the Supreme Court described the Nigerian Government's conduct in rendering him from Kenya as unlawful, but held that the illegality did not remove the Nigerian courts' jurisdiction to try him.

The result was that the prosecution was permitted to continue.

That distinction matters enormously.

The Supreme Court's position was effectively that an unlawful method of bringing a defendant before a Nigerian court did not, by itself, extinguish the court's authority to conduct the criminal proceedings.

Then Came the Kenyan High Court Judgment

Something further, and very important, happened on 24 June 2025.

The High Court of Kenya examined what had happened to Kanu on Kenyan territory.

It found that his abduction, incommunicado detention, torture and forcible removal from Kenya violated his rights.

The court held that the Kenyan Bill of Rights applied to him while he was within Kenya, notwithstanding questions about his immigration status, and awarded KSh10 million in general damages.

This means that the unlawfulness of what happened in Kenya is no longer merely a claim made by Kanu, his family, IPOB or his legal representatives.

There is a Kenyan judicial finding concerning what occurred on Kenyan soil.

Two Different Legal Questions, Not One

This history reveals why two separate legal questions must be kept distinct.

1. Was the way Kanu was seized, detained and removed from Kenya lawful?

The Kenyan High Court found serious violations arising from his abduction, detention, torture and forcible removal.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention likewise concluded that Kanu had been subjected to extraordinary rendition and arbitrary detention.

So, on this question, there are clear findings from both the Kenyan judiciary and the UN Working Group concerning the unlawfulness of what occurred.

2. Does that illegality legally prevent Nigeria from subsequently prosecuting him?

Nigeria's Supreme Court ultimately held that it did not.

The Court concluded in December 2023 that the unlawful manner in which Kanu had been returned to Nigeria did not deprive the Nigerian courts of jurisdiction to continue the criminal proceedings against him.

Those two questions should never be conflated.

Finding that the method used to bring someone before a court was unlawful is not necessarily the same legal question as deciding whether that court may subsequently prosecute him.

Nigeria's Supreme Court treated those as separate issues.

Whether that conclusion was legally correct is among the matters that may continue to be debated and challenged through lawful appellate processes. But the present position must be described accurately: the Supreme Court allowed the prosecution to continue.

Why Johal's Bail Does Not Automatically Translate Into Kanu's Release

Johal's case before the Delhi High Court centred heavily on prolonged incarceration without completion of the trial.

The court recorded that he had been imprisoned since November 2017, that only 40 witnesses had been examined and that approximately 123 were still to testify. It concluded that the proceedings were not likely to end soon.

Johal therefore came before the court as a defendant who had spent more than eight years imprisoned without conviction in the cases concerned.

Kanu's current position is different.

He is challenging an existing conviction and sentence.

His appeal, filed in February 2026, raises several arguments, including complaints about the conduct of the trial, unresolved preliminary objections, fair-hearing protections and the legislation under which he says he was convicted. These are his grounds of appeal; they have not yet become determinations in his favour by the Court of Appeal.

That legal distinction helps explain why the two cases can presently produce different bail outcomes.

It does not, however, erase the separate findings surrounding Kanu's extraordinary rendition.

Both things can be true at once.

What About the British Government?

This is where another important comparison arises.

The UK Government has repeatedly raised Johal's case with India.

On 1 July 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office told Parliament that the Foreign Secretary had raised Johal's case with Indian counterparts on several occasions, most recently during a visit to India in early June. The Government said it continued to tell India that faster progress was required towards a full resolution.

A further parliamentary answer on 10 July said the UK was continuing to press for progress and a swift resolution and confirmed that the Foreign Secretary had discussed the case with her Indian counterpart on 4 June.

The UK Government has also raised Mazi Nnamdi Kanu's case with Nigeria.

In a parliamentary answer dated 19 November 2025, the FCDO said ministers had raised Kanu's case with the Nigerian authorities on multiple occasions, most recently when the Minister for Africa met Nigerian Foreign Minister Yusuf Tuggar on 11 November 2025. It also said consular officials visited Kanu, attended his court hearings and remained in contact with his family and legal representatives.

When Parliament asked again in January 2026 what representations the Government had made and what it was doing to secure Kanu's release, the FCDO's February response referred MPs back to that November 2025 answer.

So it would not be accurate to say that the British Government has never raised Kanu's case.

It has.

The question his family and supporters continue to ask is what further diplomatic action the Government is prepared to take in light of his British citizenship, the UN Working Group's findings and the Kenyan High Court judgment.

That question remains especially important to us.

And Margaret Continues to Ask the Questions That Must Be Asked

This brings me to someone I must acknowledge personally.

Margaret @margieOBE, thank you.

You never seem to relent in your efforts to represent us.

Whenever we meet with, write to or communicate with the government departments dealing with this case, you continue to ask difficult questions and press for answers.

Margaret, thank you for your constant representation of my family.

Thank you for the persistent pressure you apply in calling for the release of my husband, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu.

Thank you for the doors you knock on and for the roads you somehow continue to find when it seems there is nowhere else to turn.

Last night, at almost midnight, you were still emailing me asking for an update.

That says so much about who you are.

Even at that hour, you were still thinking, still questioning and still searching for another avenue through which the Government could be challenged to respond.

Your courage, persistence and kind words mean more to me than I can adequately express.

The encouragement I receive from you fuels me.

And I know that I will spend the rest of my life fighting for others with the same consciousness, compassion and determination that you have shown us.

You have continued to support and represent us without asking for, or receiving, anything from me in return.

You get on the bus and go wherever we need to be.

You turn up.

You write.

You question.

You challenge.

You follow up.

And you refuse to allow uncomfortable questions to disappear simply because those in authority would rather not answer them, just as you roared at the Prisoner 951 gathering.

You are a powerful and conscious soul.

You are a warrior.

Keep the fire burning, Margaret.

The Bottom Line

Johal and Kanu are both British citizens.

Both cases have involved lengthy detention, terrorism-related prosecutions, international human-rights scrutiny and UK consular involvement.

But their current procedural positions are materially different.

Johal has obtained bail after more than eight years of largely pre-trial detention in proceedings that remain unfinished.

Kanu has been convicted and is now pursuing an appeal and bail application while the conviction and sentence remain operative.

At the same time, Kanu's case contains an additional and extraordinary legal history: his forcible movement from Kenya into Nigeria, the UN Working Group's finding of extraordinary rendition, Nigeria's Supreme Court judgment permitting his prosecution to continue despite illegality surrounding his return, and the Kenyan High Court's subsequent findings concerning his abduction, incommunicado detention, torture and unlawful removal.

That history cannot simply be erased because a later conviction occurred.

Nor should different legal questions be collapsed into one.

The legality of his rendition, the legality of his subsequent prosecution and the validity of his eventual conviction are related, but legally distinct, issues.

And now his appeal must take its course.

For my family, however, the human question remains just as real as the legal one.

We continue to seek answers.

We continue to seek action.

We continue to stand.

We fight for truth in consciousness, with courage and persistence.

And no matter how long the road may be, the truth must prevail.

DELHI UNION OF JOURNALISTS (Regd.)
Email: duj.delhi@gmail.com

19 September, 2026
Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

Sd/-

 A.M. Jigeesh, General Secretary

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

I had no option left except calling the police.

“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Dear @noidapolice, @CMOfficeUP the CCTNS portal has multiple issues. I tried filing for tenant verification form online and it challenged me, in some ways saying, “Let me see, how the hell can you file this request, I will show you how sarkari I am!” 

1. Permanent address is pre-selected to UP, meaning I have to put a false UP address to move to next page

2. For a simple jpg file upload, under the recommended size, it kept on returning ‘malicious script found’. Finally, I had to use photoshop, to remove all metadata etc, rename the file and so on! 

3. The tenant info page has two mandatory boxes- Relative name and Relation - can’t write ‘self’, because in ‘relation’ drop down, there is no such thing. 

4. This one is good: After an hour of filling the form, when you hit submit, it goes to ‘processing’ and returns to ‘submit’. I ‘submitted’ it thrice and then thought ‘it must have been submitted. Guess what! No. It doesn’t exist now. No application ID, no service request number, nothing! 

Finally, I asked my property dealer how long it takes for verification, and he was like ‘Sir, kal karwa dunga. Aap ₹500 per person de dena.’ 

I have no choice but to give the details to him for offline application. There is no doubt Digital India is doing wonders, but for some places, the more things change, the more they remain the same. 

No doubt, Noida Police is doing a tremendous job, and I had no intent on tagging them, but this comes under their jurisdiction. Please ask the agency handling it, to make it smooth. I don’t have issues waiting for it to process, but it must do the job efficiently. 

Cc: @ChiefSecyUP @myogiadityanath
